newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK transport firm shares in election jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK transport firm shares in election jitters.

text.p: Shares in British transport group Stagecoach Plc suffered a major bout of pre-election jitters on Wednesday, crashing five percent amid growing fears of a regulatory clampdown.

Stagecoach, owner of privatised South West Trains (SWT), which faces the threat of a one million pounds ($1.6 million) fine for cancelled services, saw its share price fall by 38-1/2 pence to 685 by 1600 GMT after touching a low of 675.
The shares have fallen steadily in recent weeks from a high of 804 pence.

Traders said that with the opposition Labour Party well ahead in the opinion polls, investors were panicking that a future Labour government could impose a harsh regulatory regime if it wins the election set for May 1.
After 18 years of Conservative rule, during which privatisation of the railways and other public companies has been a key policy, transport could be a flashpoint in the election campaign.
Transport stocks have had a bonanza year but the stock market's enthusiasm has recently been tempered by political caution.

Andrew Smith, Labour's shadow Transport Secretary, told Reuters last week he planned a regulatory bite-back, particularly for rail infrastructure group Railtrack Plc and the rail operation franchises including South West Trains.

Earlier this week Labour unnerved market sentiment further when shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown indicated that Railtrack would be caught by its planned one-off windfall tax on privatised utilities.
It has argued in the past that Railtrack was sold off too cheaply last May.
Since then its shares have rocketed from around 220-1/2 pence to a high of 501 before falling back to the current 464 level.
One analyst said he believed that the windfall tax issue was not enough to detract from Railtrack's value on a major scale.
"Even if the windfall tax was up to 200 million (pounds), Railtrack could afford it and take it on the chin," he said.

Asked about Labour's threat to alter the terms governing Railtrack's income source -- track access charges -- or stipulate investment targets, the analyst said, "That would require primary legislation. It would send the wrong kind of message to investors here and abroad if a government breaks up legal contracts."
But analysts concede that the rail franchises, which run passenger services, could face tougher penalties for transgressions.
"The penalty regime is not being used to the full. One of the proofs is the South West Trains affair," Labour's Smith said.
Pressure from consumer groups for tougher regulation continues to mount, with lobby groups calling for tough action against rail service operators like MTL Ltd and Prism Rail for cancelled trains.

Even though these are not on the scale of South West Trains, which has cancelled more than 2,500 trains in eight weeks after a job-reduction programme left it short of drivers, the regulator Opraf says every privatisation "teething problem" is being magnified in the run-up to the election as political point-scoring intensifies. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
